title: Book of the Dead, Spell 31: Stopping those who come to take away the Spells [or Mind] of a Person ... (papyrus of Iuefankh)
source: Papyrus of Iuefankh, Turin, Museo Egizio Cat. 1791 (Museo Egizio photographs, CC0) + TLA transliteration (ed. B. Backes, CC BY-SA 4.0) + English of Samuel Birch (1867, public domain)
description: Spell 31 of the Book of the Dead in the Turin papyrus of Iuefankh (Ptolemaic period): stopping those who come to take away the Spells [or Mind] of a Person ..., with the TLA transliteration and Birch's 1867 English.
introduction:
The Book of the Dead, in Egyptian the spells for going forth by day, is a collection of funerary spells written on papyrus rolls and placed in burials from the New Kingdom to the Roman period. Each roll was made for one person, with spells taken from a large repertoire and illustrated with drawings (vignettes). This library gives one complete roll: the papyrus of Iuefankh in the Museo Egizio, Turin (Cat. 1791), written in the Ptolemaic period (332-30 BCE) and coming from Thebes. Richard Lepsius published it in 1842 and divided it into 165 chapters; his numbering is still the standard numbering of the spells, and it is used here.

Spell 31 (Birch: 'The chapter of Stopping those who come to take away the Spells [or Mind] of a Person from him in Hades.') is on Lepsius's plate XVI and on photographs 6, 7 of the 31 Museo Egizio photographs of the roll.

The Egyptian is the transliteration of the Thesaurus Linguae Aegyptiae (edition by Burkhard Backes), with the column number of the spell before each column; the numbers are those of Lepsius's plates. On the papyrus the text runs in vertical columns of cursive hieroglyphs from right to left along the roll; titles and some words are written in red. Signs restored by the editor are in square brackets, signs the scribe left out in angle brackets, superfluous signs in braces and damaged signs in half brackets. The English is the translation by Samuel Birch, published in 1867 and made from Lepsius's copy of this papyrus, so the English and the Egyptian come from the same manuscript. It was the first complete English translation of the Book of the Dead; many passages are now understood differently. Birch's own square brackets give his alternatives and explanations. The photographs are by the Museo Egizio; each shows a stretch of the roll, and the note of each section says where the spell stands on it.
translator_notes: Birch's English was taken from three scans of Bunsen's Egypt's Place in Universal History, vol. V (1867), on the Internet Archive. The three OCR texts were aligned word by word and each word was settled by their agreement; running heads, page numbers, footnote markers and footnotes were removed. Some OCR errors may remain, chiefly in proper names.
Birch uses the terms and name forms of his time: Hades, Aahlu (Elysium), Tum for Atum, Seb for Geb, Anup for Anubis, Phoenix or Bennu for the heron.
Labels such as 'title line' or 'gate 1' before a line of the Egyptian translate the position labels of the TLA.
The TLA has no hieroglyphic encoding for these texts, so only the transliteration is shown.

translation.text:
XXXI. The chapter of Stopping those who come to take away the Spells [or Mind] of a Person from him in Hades.

Vignette. — Deceased turning back four Crocodiles.]

Stop, go back! Back, Crocodile, from coming to me. I know by my mind [or spells]. Do not thou say the name of the Great God. Thou who lettest the Emis-saries come is one name. Ape [Ben] is one name. At the true angle, Turner back of the Paths of Heaven, or Turner in the Heaven at the hour; Turner back of the Violent [or millions]. He has taken the stealers of my spells [mind]. My hard tooth eats the beseechers. in the Land of. .. Oh seated! [having] a [date] weakness in his eye at this mind [or spell], annihilate these crocodiles who live off his spells [or brain]. I am he who dwells in the Fields, I am [he]. I am Osiris who shut up his father Seb and his mother Nu, the day of the great battle. My father is Seb, my mother is Nu. I am Horus the preferred, the day of the rising. I am Anup in the day of judgment. I am the [one or he] who is Osiris, the going Chief. The word [saying] to Abuskhau [to the palette and paper], the doorkeeper of Osiris, because I myself have come, I perceive, I judge, I prevail, I have come, I have defended myself, I have sat in the birthplace of Osiris, born with him, I renew myself like him. I have introduced the leg into the place where Osiris is: I open the Gate of the Gods who are there. I have sat at his place, having my tongue and mouth satisfied with [writing].

Thousands of food, of drink off the table of his father Osiris, of bullocks, of pure cattle, of bulls, of herons, of ducks, of geese, destroyed by Horus, sacrificed by Thoth. I repose exceedingly well. I have welcomed at the altar of the ruler of Tattu. I am in his place. I blow the East wind on his head, I hold the West wind in his breast. I have gone round the four quarters in the heaven. I have made the South wind to touch his hair. I give winds to the Blessed, that they may eat the bread.

If this chapter is known, he comes out from [or as] the day, he is walking off earth from amongst the living, he never wastes in pure linen, for millions of times.
translation.scan_note: Turin 1791, Spell 31 (TLA Tb 031: title line, columns 1-12; Lepsius 1842, pl. XVI). Photograph 6 of 31 (Commons Book_of_the_Dead_of_Iuefankh,_papyrus_-_Museo_Egizio_Turin_C_1791_p029.jpg): its vignette of a man spearing crocodiles begins at the left-hand edge (0-6%); it continues on photograph 7. Photograph 7 of 31 (Commons Book_of_the_Dead_of_Iuefankh,_papyrus_-_Museo_Egizio_Turin_C_1791_p028.jpg): the man spearing crocodiles and its columns at 76-95%. Checked by eye: the photographs were matched to Lepsius's plates by their vignettes, red titles and framed compartments, and the overlapping edges of neighbouring photographs were compared.

Positions in the notes are measured from the left edge of the photograph.
